# Connected2Country

> Aboriginal-owned consultancy. Consultant anthropologist and archaeologist of Aboriginal descent (Helen Haritos) based in Darwin, Northern Territory, Australia. Provides Traditional Owner and Native Title holder consultation, AAPA Authority Certificate support and sacred site advice, cultural heritage and cultural values assessments, Cultural Heritage Management Plans and CEMP heritage sections, native title and anthropological research and expert reports, cultural awareness inductions and ceremony facilitation, and AI/digital services for cultural heritage including Indigenous Data Sovereignty advice. Over 20 years in NT Aboriginal land, heritage and native title work, including senior anthropologist roles with the Northern Land Council and Tiwi Land Council. Phone 0438 805 294. Email helen@connected2country.au. ABN 23 319 539 776.

Service regions in priority order: (1) Darwin, Palmerston and the Litchfield rural area (Larrakia country); (2) the Top End including Katherine, Kakadu, Arnhem Land, the Tiwi Islands and the Daly; (3) the wider Northern Territory and the East Kimberley region of Western Australia (Kununurra, Wyndham, Halls Creek).

# Traditional Owner and Native Title holder consultation
URL: https://connected2country.au/services/traditional-owner-consultation/

Most heritage, sacred site, planning and environmental approvals in the Territory come back to the same question: have the right Traditional Owners been asked, properly, and is there a record of what they said? I work out who speaks for the Country in question, set up a process that suits them rather than the project program, run the meetings and site visits, and write it up in a form that AAPA, the land councils, the Heritage Branch and lawyers will accept.

Included:
- Identification of Traditional Owners, custodians and Native Title holders for the project area, drawing on land council, AAPA, Native Title and published anthropological records
- Consultation design: who, where, in what order, with what information, and how consent or objection is recorded
- Facilitation of meetings, on-Country site visits and family-group discussions, with interpreters and cultural advisers where needed
- Consultation registers, meeting records, consent and conditions documentation suitable for EIS, AAPA, Heritage Branch and Development Consent Authority submissions
- Ongoing liaison through construction, including cultural monitors and incident response
- Advice on engagement under the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976, the Native Title Act 1993 and land council processes

Who it is for: Developers, civil head contractors and project managers with a Darwin or Top End project that needs Traditional Owner input; heritage and environmental consultancies that need a Darwin-based anthropologist for the consultation component; NT Government agencies, Defence contractors and utilities.
Pricing: Scoped and quoted before work starts. Defined consultation programs are fixed price; open-ended engagement is on an agreed day rate with meeting payments and interpreter costs at cost.

FAQ:
Q: Who are the Traditional Owners for Darwin?
A: The Larrakia people are the recognised Traditional Owners of the Darwin region, including Darwin, Palmerston and much of the rural area. Who speaks for a specific place within Larrakia country, and for places on the margins of neighbouring estates, is a matter for proper anthropological inquiry rather than a single list, which is what the consultation process establishes.
Q: Is Traditional Owner consultation legally required?
A: It depends on the approval pathway. AAPA Authority Certificates are issued on the basis of consultation with custodians; works on Aboriginal land require land council and Traditional Owner consent under the Land Rights Act; NT EPA assessments and Development Consent Authority processes expect it; and Native Title future act processes require notification or negotiation. Even where it is not a formal requirement, documented consultation is the single best protection against delay later.
Q: How long does consultation take?
A: Allow six to twelve weeks for a typical Darwin development, longer for remote communities or where sorry business, ceremony or the Wet season affects availability. Early engagement is the only reliable way to shorten the critical path.


# AAPA Authority Certificate support and sacred site advice
URL: https://connected2country.au/services/aapa-authority-certificate-sacred-sites/

If your works could affect a sacred site, an Authority Certificate from AAPA is the only thing that protects you under the Sacred Sites Act. I have been on both sides of these: on sacred site surveys with AAPA and custodians while at the land councils, and helping proponents apply, make sense of the conditions and keep the site crew inside them.

Included:
- Pre-application advice: whether a certificate is needed, what area to apply over and how to describe the works to avoid re-applications
- Desktop review of AAPA register abstracts, previous certificates and anthropological literature for the project area
- Support to custodian consultation and sacred site surveys, including attendance on Country
- Plain-English interpretation of Authority Certificate conditions, restricted work areas and buffers for engineers and site supervisors
- Sacred site awareness inductions, site marking protocols and compliance inspections during construction
- Advice on variations, amendments and incidents, and on registering sites where custodians request it

Who it is for: Developers and contractors applying for or working under an Authority Certificate in Darwin, Palmerston, the rural area and across the NT; environmental consultants preparing EIS culture and heritage chapters; NT Government and Defence project teams.
Pricing: Pre-application advice and desktop reviews are fixed price. Consultation support and construction compliance are on an agreed day rate.

FAQ:
Q: Do I need an AAPA Authority Certificate for my development?
A: If your works could affect a sacred site, a certificate is the only way to be sure you are protected. In practice, most subdivisions, infrastructure projects and works near the coast, waterways, rock outcrops or significant trees in the Darwin region apply for one. AAPA charges fees based on project value; we can advise before you apply whether the application is worth it and how to scope it.
Q: What is a restricted work area?
A: A restricted work area (RWA) is an area defined in an Authority Certificate within which particular works are prohibited or conditioned to protect a sacred site. Conditions commonly limit ground disturbance, vegetation clearing, access or vehicle movement. The site itself is confidential; the RWA is what the proponent must manage.
Q: Can Connected2Country issue a sacred site clearance?
A: No. Only AAPA issues Authority Certificates. Connected2Country prepares you for the application, supports the custodian consultation and helps you comply with the conditions.


# Cultural heritage and cultural values assessments
URL: https://connected2country.au/services/cultural-heritage-assessment/

Cultural heritage is not just the archaeology. Places carry story, kinship, ecological knowledge and living use that never show up in a shovel test. I assess those values with the people who hold them, alongside the archaeological places the Heritage Act protects, and write it up so planners, EIS assessors and, if it comes to it, courts can use it.

Included:
- Desktop cultural heritage assessments: register searches, literature review, previous surveys and constraints mapping
- Ethnographic and cultural values assessments with Traditional Owners, including intangible values, story, kinship and ecological knowledge
- Archaeological survey coordination and field recording, with specialist archaeologists engaged for larger programs
- Culture and heritage chapters for NT EPA environmental impact statements and referrals
- Heritage Act 2011 advice: declared places, heritage significance, works approvals and Heritage Council submissions
- Ethno-ecology research linking cultural values to flora, fauna, water and seasonal use

Who it is for: Proponents of subdivisions, infrastructure, Defence, energy and resource projects; environmental consultancies that need the heritage component delivered locally; land councils and Aboriginal corporations documenting values on their own Country.
Pricing: Desktop assessments are fixed price. Field assessments are quoted on area, access and number of Traditional Owner participants.

FAQ:
Q: What is the difference between the Heritage Act and the Sacred Sites Act?
A: The Heritage Act 2011 (NT) protects declared heritage places and objects, plus all Aboriginal and Macassan archaeological places and objects, and is administered by the Heritage Branch. The Northern Territory Aboriginal Sacred Sites Act 1989 protects sacred sites, which are places of significance under Aboriginal tradition, and is administered by AAPA. A project often needs to deal with both.
Q: Do you do archaeology as well as anthropology?
A: Yes. Helen Haritos holds an honours degree in archaeology and has conducted archaeological surveys in the NT, and partners with specialist archaeologists for larger programs. Most Top End projects need both disciplines working together.
Q: Can the assessment be used in an EIS?
A: Yes. Assessments are written to NT EPA environmental factor guidance for culture and heritage and are structured so they drop straight into an EIS or referral.


# Cultural Heritage Management Plans and CEMP heritage sections
URL: https://connected2country.au/services/cultural-heritage-management-plans/

Getting the approval is one thing; living with its conditions for two years of construction is another. I write heritage management plans that a site supervisor can actually follow, then do the inductions, monitoring and inspections that show the conditions were met.

Included:
- Cultural Heritage Management Plans tied to Authority Certificate conditions, Heritage Act approvals and Traditional Owner agreements
- Cultural heritage sections and procedures for Construction Environmental Management Plans
- Unexpected finds and ancestral remains procedures
- Site induction content and delivery for crews and subcontractors
- Cultural monitor programs with Traditional Owners during ground disturbance
- Compliance inspections, audits and close-out reporting for superintendents and regulators

Who it is for: Civil head contractors and subcontractors on NT Government, Defence, utility and private development contracts; developers passing approval conditions down to contractors; environmental consultants preparing CEMPs who need the heritage component.
Pricing: Plans are fixed price for defined scopes. Inductions, monitoring and inspections are on an agreed day rate or per-visit price.

FAQ:
Q: Does my CEMP need a cultural heritage section?
A: Almost always. NT Government, Defence and most private contract environmental clauses require the CEMP to address heritage and sacred sites, and any Authority Certificate or Heritage Act condition has to be translated into site controls. A generic paragraph will not satisfy a superintendent.
Q: What happens if we find artefacts or remains during works?
A: Stop work in the immediate area, protect the find and notify the Heritage Branch (and police for suspected human remains). Your plan should say exactly who does what. Connected2Country responds to unexpected finds across the Darwin region and advises remotely elsewhere.
Q: Can you work with our existing environmental consultant?
A: Yes. Connected2Country regularly provides the heritage component to environmental consultancies, including Bell Enviro, so that one integrated plan goes to the client.


# Anthropological research, native title support and expert reports
URL: https://connected2country.au/services/anthropological-research-expert-reports/

I spent more than a decade as a regional and then senior anthropologist with the Northern Land Council, two years with the Tiwi Land Council, and before that worked in the NT Government unit that handled exploration and mining on Aboriginal land. I also did the ANU native title research placement with Julie Finlayson and Nicholas Peterson. That is the background I bring to research briefs from land councils, Aboriginal corporations, lawyers and government.

Included:
- Native title connection research, genealogies and claim group descriptions
- Land claim and Aboriginal Land Rights (NT) Act 1976 research, including section 19 lease and consent processes
- Independent anthropological reports and peer reviews for lawyers, land councils and tribunals
- Traditional Owner identification and succession advice for agreements, royalties and distributions
- Historical, archival and museum collection research, including repatriation and provenance of cultural objects
- Culturally informed advice to boards, corporations and government on governance and decision-making

Who it is for: Land councils and Native Title representative bodies, Aboriginal corporations and PBCs, law firms, NT and Commonwealth agencies, museums and research institutions.
Pricing: Research is quoted per brief, usually as a capped number of days with milestones.

FAQ:
Q: Can you act as an expert witness?
A: Helen Haritos prepares independent anthropological reports to the standard expected of an expert and can give evidence where required. Each brief is assessed for conflicts before acceptance.
Q: Do you work outside the Northern Territory?
A: The practice is NT-focused with capacity for the East Kimberley region of Western Australia, where Helen has lived and worked. International archival research has been undertaken in Europe for Tiwi cultural objects.
Q: How is confidential cultural information handled?
A: Restricted information stays with the people it belongs to. Reports distinguish between what can be published and what must remain confidential, and data is stored and shared under agreed protocols.


# Cultural awareness training, heritage inductions and ceremony facilitation
URL: https://connected2country.au/services/cultural-awareness-inductions/

In my experience, heritage incidents on construction sites are rarely malicious. Somebody did not know the buffer was there, or what the certificate condition meant for their excavator. A half-day induction built around the actual project, its Authority Certificate and the people whose Country it is on fixes most of that, and starts the relationship with Traditional Owners on the right foot.

Included:
- Project-specific cultural heritage and sacred site inductions for site crews, delivered on site or online
- Cultural awareness sessions for project teams, boards and government staff, grounded in the Country the project is on
- Facilitation of Welcome to Country, smoking ceremonies and site openings with the appropriate Traditional Owners, including payments and logistics
- Protocols for working with Traditional Owners, cultural monitors and communities
- Induction records and attendance registers for compliance files

Who it is for: Head contractors mobilising a Darwin or Top End site, developers launching a project, government agencies and corporate teams working on Aboriginal land or with Aboriginal organisations.
Pricing: Inductions and sessions are priced per session; ceremony facilitation is priced per event with Traditional Owner payments passed through at cost.

FAQ:
Q: How do we arrange a Welcome to Country in Darwin?
A: A Welcome to Country should be given by a Larrakia Traditional Owner. Connected2Country identifies the right person for the location and occasion, agrees the fee, and handles the logistics so that the event is respectful and the relationship is sound.
Q: Is a cultural induction the same as a general cultural awareness course?
A: No. A general course explains culture in the abstract. A project induction tells your crew which areas are restricted, what the Authority Certificate conditions mean on the ground, who the Traditional Owners are and what to do if something is found. Both have a place; the induction is the one that protects the project.


# AI and digital services for cultural heritage
URL: https://connected2country.au/services/ai-digital-cultural-heritage/

I use AI tools for the desktop side of heritage work: reading registers and old reports, drafting from field notes, keeping registers current. It makes that part faster and cheaper. It does not replace going on Country or talking to people, and it raises real questions about where cultural knowledge ends up. I help Traditional Owner organisations set the rules for that, and help proponents and consultancies use the tools without embarrassing themselves.

Included:
- AI-assisted desktop assessments: rapid review of registers, reports, literature and archives, verified by the anthropologist before anything is relied on
- Digital recording and archiving of cultural knowledge, oral histories and collections, with access controls set by custodians
- Indigenous Data Sovereignty and AI governance advice for land councils, Aboriginal corporations and ranger groups, aligned with CARE principles and Maiam nayri Wingara guidance
- Advice to proponents and consultancies on what AI can and cannot do in heritage compliance, and what regulators and Traditional Owners will accept
- Digitisation and cataloguing support for community museums, keeping places and archives, building on work with the Patakijiyali Museum on the Tiwi Islands
- Plain-language cultural protocols for AI use within organisations working with Aboriginal knowledge

Who it is for: Aboriginal corporations, land councils and ranger groups deciding how their knowledge is handled; museums and keeping places; environmental and heritage consultancies and proponents who want faster desktop work without compromising the fieldwork.
Pricing: Advisory work is quoted per brief. AI-assisted desktop assessments are fixed price and typically cost less than conventional desktop studies.

FAQ:
Q: Can AI replace an anthropologist for Traditional Owner consultation?
A: No. Consultation is a relationship between people about Country, and the legal and cultural weight of the outcome rests on that. AI is useful for the desktop work around it: finding and summarising what has already been recorded, drafting documents from field notes, and keeping registers current.
Q: What is Indigenous Data Sovereignty?
A: The right of Indigenous peoples to govern the collection, ownership and application of data about their people, lands, knowledge and resources. For cultural heritage it means custodians decide what is recorded, who holds it, who can see it and whether it may be used to train or query AI systems.
Q: Is cultural information safe in AI tools?
A: Only if the tool, the contract and the workflow are chosen for it. Public AI services may retain and reuse inputs. Connected2Country advises on tools and settings that do not train on your data, on what should never be entered at all, and on written protocols so staff know the difference.

# What is an AAPA Authority Certificate and do I need one?
URL: https://connected2country.au/guides/what-is-an-aapa-authority-certificate/

An Authority Certificate is a document issued by the Aboriginal Areas Protection Authority (AAPA) under the Northern Territory Aboriginal Sacred Sites Act 1989 . It sets out the conditions under which proposed works can proceed without damaging or interfering with a sacred site, and it is a complete defence to prosecution under the Act if the works stay within those conditions. Why it matters Sacred sites are protected everywhere in the Northern Territory, on all tenures, whether or not they are registered and whether or not you know they are there. Damaging one is a criminal offence with penalties for both the company and individuals. The certificate is the only way to know in advance where the constraints are. When to apply Any ground-disturbing works where sacred sites are plausible: coastal land, rivers and creeks, springs, rock outcrops, significant trees, and most undeveloped land around Darwin and Palmerston. When a development permit, NT EPA approval, land council agreement or contract requires it. When your financier, principal or insurer asks for it, which is increasingly common. How the process works Application to AAPA with a description of the works and a map of the area. Fees are set against project value. AAPA checks its register and records and consults the custodians of any sites in or near the area, usually with field visits. AAPA issues the certificate with conditions, often including restricted work areas (RWAs) with buffers and limits on particular activities. The proponent builds the conditions into its management plans, inductions and site controls. Common mistakes Applying over too small an area, then needing a new certificate when the design changes. Describing the works too narrowly, so that laydown areas, haul roads or borrow pits are not covered. Treating the certificate as a tick-box and never translating the conditions for the site crew. Leaving the application until after the program is set. Custodian consultation takes the time it takes. Connected2Country helps proponents scope the application, supports the custodian consultation and turns the conditions into something a site supervisor can work to. See AAPA Authority Certificate support .

# Do I need Traditional Owner consultation for my Darwin development?
URL: https://connected2country.au/guides/traditional-owner-consultation-darwin-development/

For most development in the greater Darwin region the answer is yes, and the real question is how much and how early. The Larrakia people are the recognised Traditional Owners of the Darwin region, and several approval pathways either require their involvement or work far better with it. Approvals that expect consultation AAPA Authority Certificates are issued on the basis of consultation with custodians of sacred sites. NT EPA assessment of significant projects requires the proponent to assess impacts on culture and heritage, which cannot be done credibly without talking to Traditional Owners. Heritage Act 2011 processes for Aboriginal archaeological places and declared heritage places involve the Heritage Council and, in practice, Traditional Owner views. Native Title future act procedures apply where native title has not been extinguished. Planning Act processes for rezoning and large subdivisions increasingly expect evidence of consultation, and Crown land and Darwin Waterfront, Defence and Commonwealth processes have their own requirements. Who to consult Identifying the right people is anthropological work, not a mailing list. Larrakia country has family groups with particular connections to particular places, and some areas on the edges of the region are shared with or claimed by neighbouring groups. Getting this wrong is the most common reason consultation is later challenged. What good consultation looks like Started early, before the design is fixed. Plain information about what is proposed, with maps and site visits. Time for people to talk among themselves and come back. Records that show who was consulted, what they said and what changed as a result. Fair payment for people's time and expertise. Connected2Country runs this process for developers and contractors across Darwin, Palmerston and the rural area. See Traditional Owner consultation .

# NT heritage laws explained: Sacred Sites Act, Heritage Act and the Land Rights Act
URL: https://connected2country.au/guides/nt-heritage-laws-explained/

Three pieces of legislation do most of the work in protecting Aboriginal cultural heritage in the Northern Territory. Projects often need to deal with more than one. Northern Territory Aboriginal Sacred Sites Act 1989 Protects sacred sites, which are places of significance under Aboriginal tradition, on all land in the Territory. Administered by the Aboriginal Areas Protection Authority (AAPA), which keeps a register, consults custodians and issues Authority Certificates. Offences apply whether or not a site is registered. Heritage Act 2011 (NT) Protects declared heritage places and objects, and gives automatic protection to all Aboriginal and Macassan archaeological places and objects. Administered by the Heritage Branch with advice from the NT Heritage Council. Works that may affect a protected place need approval, and unexpected finds must be reported. Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 (Cth) Grants inalienable freehold title to Aboriginal land trusts over roughly half of the Territory and requires that Traditional Owners consent, through the relevant land council, to leases, mining and other uses of that land. Section 19 leases and section 42 to 48 mining provisions are the parts proponents meet most often. Land councils employ anthropologists to identify Traditional Owners and run consultations. And the rest The Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) applies where native title survives on non-Aboriginal land; the Environment Protection Act 2019 (NT) requires culture and heritage to be assessed for significant projects; and the Commonwealth Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act 1984 is a last-resort protection. How they fit together on a project A subdivision on freehold land near the Darwin coast might need an AAPA Authority Certificate, a Heritage Act check for archaeological places, and Traditional Owner consultation for the NT EPA or planning process. A road on Aboriginal land near Maningrida needs land council consent under the Land Rights Act plus the certificate. Working out the pathway early is most of the value an anthropologist adds. See cultural heritage assessment .

# AI in cultural heritage work: what changes and what does not
URL: https://connected2country.au/guides/ai-in-cultural-heritage-what-changes/

AI tools can now read a decade of heritage reports in an afternoon, draft a management plan from field notes, transcribe interviews and keep registers current. That changes the economics of desktop work. It does not change what gives heritage work its legal and cultural weight. What AI does well Finding and summarising what has already been recorded about a place across registers, reports, archives and literature. Drafting documents from the anthropologist's field notes, so that the human time goes into the fieldwork and the judgement. Transcribing and indexing oral histories, with custodian control over access. Keeping consultation registers, condition registers and compliance records current. What stays with people Identifying who speaks for Country. This is relationship and knowledge, and the answer is contested often enough that it must be defensible. Consultation itself. Consent given to a person on Country is what regulators, courts and communities recognise. Assessing significance and giving expert opinion. Deciding what knowledge is recorded at all, and what must stay restricted. The risks Confidential cultural information entered into public AI services that retain and reuse inputs. Fluent, confident summaries of sources that do not say what the summary claims. Every AI output in heritage work needs verification against the source. Reports that look complete but were never checked by someone who has been on the Country. Organisations adopting tools with no protocol, so staff make the decisions by accident. Questions to ask Who owns the data? Where is it stored and is it used for training? Who verified the output? What is the protocol for restricted knowledge? Would the Traditional Owners whose knowledge this is agree with how it is being handled? Connected2Country uses AI for the desktop work, verifies everything, and helps organisations write the rules. See AI and digital services for cultural heritage .
